title: Narasimha Avataram
body:
Narasimha Avataram

Hiranyakashipu was no ordinary king. Brother to the slain Hiranyaksha, his power had grown beyond measure, extending across the three worlds, yet he was never satisfied. He desired dominion not only over mortals but over time, fate, and death itself. Abandoning his kingdom, he went deep into the forests and performed austerities so severe that the very cosmos trembled. Alarmed by the imbalance his penance threatened, the Devas went to Brahma, who at last appeared before Hiranyakashipu and offered him a boon.
Hiranyakashipu demanded immortality, but Brahma answered that even he was not immortal and could not grant such a thing. So the asura devised a way to escape death by hedging it about with conditions: that he not be killed by man or beast, by Deva or Asura; that he die neither by day nor by night, neither inside a dwelling nor outside it, neither upon the earth nor in the sky; that no weapon forged by mortals or celestials could slay him; and that he not be killed by any being created by Brahma. Brahma granted it — knowing well that there existed One beyond his creation, beyond mortality, beyond every condition the asura had named, who would in time bring justice.
With the boon secured, Hiranyakashipu declared himself a god, ordered that he alone be worshipped, razed the temples of Narayana, and punished any who dared chant the Lord's name. But at the height of his power a son was born to him, Prahlada, a child whose destiny would unravel the empire of darkness his father had built. Even in the womb Prahlada had been blessed, for while his mother was in the care of the sage Narada, she had listened to the glories of Vishnu, and so had the unborn child. By the time he entered the world his devotion was already sealed.
Hiranyakashipu raised his son in luxury and sent him to the finest teachers, ordering that absolute loyalty be instilled in him. But no matter how often Prahlada was asked who was supreme, his answer never changed — Sriman Narayana alone. Worse, he turned his classmates toward the Lord as well, filling the minds of the young ones with His glories. Enraged, Hiranyakashipu ordered his own son killed. Prahlada was set beneath a rampaging elephant, but the beast bowed and garlanded him; he was hurled from a height, but the winds bore him gently down; he was given poison, but it turned to nectar in his mouth; and when the king's sister Holika, immune to fire, carried him into the flames, it was she who burned to ash while the boy emerged untouched.
Driven to madness, Hiranyakashipu dragged his son into the royal court and demanded to know how he survived. Prahlada answered that the Lord protected him, for the Lord was everywhere — in every atom of creation, within himself, and even within his father. When the tyrant sneered and asked whether his Lord was in the very pillar before them, Prahlada answered that He was. Hiranyakashipu struck the pillar with his mace — and a sound tore through the universe. The pillar cracked, and from it emerged a form that was neither man nor beast, neither Deva nor Asura, neither of this world nor beyond it: a being with the body of a man and the head of a lion, His mane a blazing halo, His eyes burning like a thousand suns.
With a terrifying roar Narasimha seized the tyrant. He dragged him to the threshold of the palace — neither inside nor outside — and set him upon His lap, which was neither earth nor sky. Then, at the hour of sunset, which is neither day nor night, using not a forged weapon but the divine nails of His own hands, He tore open Hiranyakashipu's stomach and ended the tyrant. Every condition of the boon was met, and every illusion of invincibility was shattered. The universe fell silent, and even the gods trembled; only Prahlada was unafraid. He stepped forward and bowed, and at the sight of the boy's unwavering devotion the Lord's rage softened. When offered any boon, Prahlada asked for nothing, for he had already received everything in the moment he beheld the Lord. Narasimha blessed him with a just and lasting reign, and the balance of dharma was restored.
There is a deeper truth in this avatara. In every age the Sudarshana Chakra, the Lord's eternal enforcer of dharma, has manifested to restore balance — as the tusks of Varaha that lifted the Earth, as the arrows of Rama that felled Ravana, as the whirling discus that ended Shishupala and Narakasura. But in Narasimha the Lord did not merely wield Sudarshana; He became it. The diamond-hard nails that tore through the tyrant's illusion of immortality were Sudarshana's own decree made flesh. It is for this reason that in praising the discus we invoke the roar of Narasimha, and that devotees recite the Sudarshana Ashtakam, composed by Swami Vedanta Desikan:

pratibhaṭaśreṇibhīṣaṇa varaguṇastomabhūṣaṇa
janibhayasthānatāraṇa jagadavasthānakāraṇa;
nikhiladuṣkarmakarśana nigamasaddharmadarśana
jaya jaya śrīsudarśana jaya jaya śrīsudarśana.

Across its eight verses the hymn salutes the Sudarshana as the terror of ranks of enemies and the ornament of noble virtues; the one who carries beings across the fear of birth and is the ground of the world's existence; the destroyer of all evil deeds and the revealer of the true dharma of the Vedas; the fierce, radiant discus encircled by flames yet the shelter of those who take refuge; pervading the three worlds, made of all power, the very form of the cosmos — and each verse closes with the refrain of victory, jaya jaya śrī sudarśana.
The fierce abode of this avatara is Ahobilam, in the Nallamala hills of Andhra Pradesh, where the Lord is said to have manifested to protect Prahlada. It is home to the shrines of the Nava Narasimha, nine forms of the Lord, among which Malola Narasimha is especially revered for His benevolence beside Sri Mahalakshmi. There too stands the Ugra Sthambham, the towering rock believed to be the very pillar from which Narasimha emerged, which pilgrims climb as an act of faith and surrender. The nine forms are recalled together in a traditional verse of meditation:

jvālā ahobilaṁ mālolaṁ krodhā kāraṇaṁ ca bhārgavam;
yogānandaṁ kṣatravaṭaṁ pāvanaṁ nava mūrtayaḥ.

These are the nine Narasimhas of Ahobilam — Jwala, Ahobila, Malola, Krodha, Karancha, Bhargava, Yogananda, Kshatravata, and Pavana — each a distinct manifestation of the Lord's grace.
